steps.explanationAfterStep: The amine adds to the carbonyl carbon just as nucleophiles add to aldehydes: a tetrahedral intermediate. Unlike an aldehyde, this carbon carries a leaving group.
The C=O bond re-forms and pushes out chloride, the best leaving group on that carbon. Addition, then elimination: substitution at C=O.
The second equivalent of methylamine is the base: it ends up as methylammonium chloride. That is why two equivalents of amine (or one plus a base such as triethylamine) are used.
Also correct: the proton can come off nitrogen before chloride leaves. Either order gives the same amide.
The C=O bond re-forms and chloride leaves: N-methylacetamide.

title: Acid chloride and amine
subtitle: Methylamine adds to acetyl chloride, chloride leaves, a second methylamine takes the proton
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 10

reactants.caption: acetyl chloride + methylamine (2 equiv.)
hintTiers: Which atom of acetyl chloride is the most electron-poor? Which atom of methylamine has a lone pair?
The nitrogen lone pair forms a bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Two arrows: chloride does not leave yet.
Nitrogen lone pair → new N–C bond to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.arrowPattern: lp N5 -> σ N5-C2; σ C2-Cl4 -> lp Cl4
misconceptions.feedbackMessage: At a C=O carbon the nucleophile adds first: the π bond moves onto oxygen and a tetrahedral intermediate forms. Chloride leaves in the next step.
The carbonyl oxygen is electron-rich. The nitrogen attacks the electron-poor carbonyl carbon.
Chlorine is not the electrophile. The carbon it is attached to is: attack the carbonyl carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon. That carbon would have five bonds: move the C=O π pair onto oxygen.

tetrahedral.caption: tetrahedral intermediate + methylamine
hintTiers: The oxygen anion can push its electrons back down to re-form C=O. Which group can carbon then lose?
Re-form the C=O π bond from an oxygen lone pair, and break the C–Cl bond with its pair going to chlorine. Two arrows.
Oxygen lone pair → C=O π bond; C–Cl bond → lone pair on chlorine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing methylamine just undoes the addition. Chloride is a much better leaving group: chloride leaves.
A methyl anion is a terrible leaving group. Of the groups on this carbon, chloride is the best one to lose.

protonated-amide.caption: protonated amide + chloride + methylamine
hintTiers: Which species in the flask is a base? Chloride is a very weak one.
The second methylamine uses its lone pair on the N–H proton; that N–H bonding pair stays on the amide nitrogen. Two arrows.
Lone pair of the free methylamine → new N–H bond to the proton on the positive nitrogen; that N–H bond → lone pair on the amide nitrogen.
protonated-amide.learnerPrompt: Remove the proton from the positive nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Chloride is the conjugate base of HCl, a very weak base. The second equivalent of methylamine is the base here.
The amide carbonyl is a poor electrophile, and the amide is already made. Use the free methylamine as a base.

neutral-tetrahedral.caption: tetrahedral intermediate (deprotonated) + methylammonium
hintTiers: The oxygen anion can re-form C=O. Which group can carbon then lose?
Re-form the C=O π bond from an oxygen lone pair, and break the C–Cl bond. Two arrows.
Oxygen lone pair → C=O π bond; C–Cl bond → lone pair on chlorine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That would throw out the amine again. Chloride is the far better leaving group.

mechanismSummary: Methylamine adds to the carbonyl carbon of acetyl chloride, giving a tetrahedral intermediate. The C=O bond re-forms and chloride leaves. A second methylamine removes the proton from nitrogen, giving N-methylacetamide and methylammonium chloride.
